evidence_for.claim: Cromwell championed liberty of conscience and religious toleration in rhetoric (e.g., his 1655 declaration that he would not persecute consciences), yet his regime enforced harsh penal laws against Catholics, banned Anglican Prayer Book worship, and transplanted Irish Catholics to Connacht under the 1652 Act for the Settlement of Ireland.
evidence_for.source: Act for the Settling of Ireland (1652); Cromwell's Declaration of the Lord Protector (1655); analyzed in John Morrill, 'Oliver Cromwell' (2007).

evidence_for.claim: Having led Parliament against Charles I's arbitrary rule and dissolution of parliaments as tyrannical, Cromwell himself forcibly dissolved the Rump Parliament in April 1653 and later the First Protectorate Parliament in 1655, and instituted the rule of the Major-Generals — replicating the personal, extra-parliamentary rule he had condemned.
evidence_for.source: Thomas Carlyle (ed.), 'Oliver Cromwell's Letters and Speeches' (1845), Speech of 22 January 1655; Blair Worden, 'The Rump Parliament 1648–1653' (1974).

evidence_against.claim: Cromwell's stated religious principles (godly reformation, providentialism, and a narrow Protestant toleration that explicitly excluded 'popery and prelacy') were in fact largely consistent with his conduct in Ireland and at home; he did not claim the universal toleration later readers project onto him, so the apparent 'gap' narrows when his own stated limits are taken seriously.
evidence_against.source: Cromwell's speech to the First Protectorate Parliament, 12 September 1654, in Carlyle (ed.), 'Letters and Speeches'; Blair Worden, 'God's Instruments: Political Conduct in the England of Oliver Cromwell' (2012).
